en: The Summary of the Meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha), composed by the Master Dignāga.
Homage to the Perfection of Wisdom!
The Perfection of Wisdom is non-dual gnosis; that is the Tathāgata.
Because they serve that purpose, the term [Perfection of Wisdom] is applied to both the text and the path, as they are to be accomplished.
The basis, the domain, the activity along with its cultivation,
the classifications, the signs, the faults, and the benefits have been proclaimed.
Faith is the factor for engagement in those who possess it; the Teacher, the assembly as witnesses, and the place and time are specified in order to establish his own authority.
For in this world, the compiler of the recitation attains authority when he speaks with witnesses, specifying the place and time.
All this enumeration of particles, the self, hearing, and so forth, is merely incidental;
indeed, the primary meanings are only thirty-two.
The sixteenfold classification of emptiness has been taught in due order by means of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*; it is to be understood through that indirect instruction.
Thus, this *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* is intended here as a condensation of the text in its stated meaning; for the meanings are exactly those as they have been explained above, without any reduction.
The Sage spoke the truth when he said, "I do not see a bodhisattva";
by this, the emptiness of the internal entities that serve as the enjoyer was declared.
Furthermore, by stating that "form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form," he has here prohibited the external sense-bases as objects of enjoyment.
In the absence of form and so forth, there would be the destruction of the characteristics that constitute the support of that body;
since this point has already been understood, the claim that "that which is seen is internal" is false.
When internal phenomena are empty, their very nature is also empty;
for the lineage (*gotra*) is considered to consist of consciousness and form, whose essence is compassion and wisdom.
By stating clearly that "a sentient being is neither arisen nor ceased," and so forth, he has indeed demonstrated the emptiness of both sentient beings and saṃsāra. (Pppa 12)
One does not perceive the qualities of a Buddha nor the qualities of a Bodhisattva;
by such statements, the Ten Powers and other attributes are shown to be empty.
Since it has been proclaimed that phenomena are each individually conceptualized,
he therefore stated that there is no ultimate reality to phenomena.
Because he effects the eradication of views such as that of a self through his great [teaching],
the Blessed One therefore proclaimed the selflessness of the person in every respect.
By proclaiming that "all phenomena are unarisen," the Knower of Reality has thus explained the selflessness of phenomena in every respect.
There is the negation of the increase and decrease of both faulty and faultless [dharmas],
as well as of conditioned and unconditioned wholesome [dharmas].
And since the wholesome factors are empty, that which pertains to them remains unimpaired;
thus, the emptiness of all distinctions is subsumed within that very [emptiness]. (Pppa 18)
By means of the ten distractions of the mind, the mind is distracted elsewhere;
it is unfit for the accomplishment of non-dual knowledge by the foolish. (Pppa 19)
In order to eliminate those [extremes] by means of mutual opposition between adversary and counter-adversary,
the *Prajñāpāramitā* text and they themselves have been shown here in a condensed form.
When the Teacher, being a Bodhisattva, dispels distraction by means of the conventional vision of the aggregates, he does so by negating the conceptualization of existence as a real entity.
By this [argument], from the opening words of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* onwards until its conclusion,
the conceptualization of non-existence must be refuted by means of affirmation (*vidhi*).
These are not statements of formal reasoning; rather, only the task itself is indicated.
The logical arguments are to be understood everywhere from the *Brahmajāla* and other sūtras.
With the detailed passage beginning "I do not see a bodhisattva," the Blessed One refutes the delusion of conceptualizing entities.
Because he does not perceive even the name, nor the range [of perception], nor likewise the activity,
nor the aggregates in any way, for that reason he does not perceive a bodhisattva.
"This is the negation of the imagined" is the summary view:
every aspect that has entered into the state of being an object of knowledge is considered imagined within the intellect.
For the teaching in the *Prajñāpāramitā* is based upon three [natures]:
the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*).
By means of terms such as "it does not exist," everything that is imagined is negated;
through similes such as "like an illusion," the dependent nature is taught.
The perfected nature is proclaimed through fourfold purification;
for in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there is no other teaching of the Buddha.
In this sequence of teaching, which serves as the antidote to the ten distractions of conceptual construction,
the three [topics] are to be understood here through both collective and individual enumeration.
Just as in the initial statement, by means of the perfected, the dependent, and the imagined,
there is the removal of distraction consisting in the conceptualization of non-existence and the conceptualization of forms.
"Therefore, by those who say, 'I do not see the Buddha nor likewise enlightenment,' the rejection of conceptual constructions is to be understood here until the conclusion. (Pppa 32)
"In form, which is empty of intrinsic nature, where or by what could there be a superimposition?"—
this refutation should be understood to apply to other statements as well.
Indeed, by teaching the statement "it is empty because of emptiness," he has expressed in every way the rejection of all conceptualizations of denial.
The Buddha is like an illusion, and likewise he is like a dream;
this same sequence should be understood by the wise in other statements as well.
The Victor is described as being like an illusion through grammatical coreferentiality;
and by such terms as "like an illusion," the dependent nature (paratantra) is expressed.
The knowledge of ordinary beings that is pure by nature is spoken of by the word "Buddha," just as a Bodhisattva is a Victor (Jina).
Having concealed its own true nature and being brought under the sway of ignorance, it appears otherwise like an illusion; yet, like a dream, it abandons its fruit.
This is said to be the negation of the conceptualizations of negation— whether regarding the erroneous manifestation of non-duality or regarding its result—
for those who engage in such negation.
Form is not logically identical with emptiness, because they are mutually contradictory;
emptiness is formless, whereas form is associated with specific characteristics.
Thus, the conceptualization of multiplicity is the sublation of the conceptualization of unity;
for nothing other than that [conceptualization] can in any way obstruct the nature of emptiness.
Since that which appears is indeed non-existent, it is produced by ignorance;
it is called "ignorance" precisely because of its power to manifest what is non-existent.
This very thing is called both "form" and "perfection of wisdom";
it is non-dual, yet it appears as dual, thereby subduing the two-fold conceptual construction.
And he states the reasoning: "Because of purity, because of non-perception, and because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence, one does not perceive even multiplicity."
This form is a mere name, for in reality it is without intrinsic nature;
thus, it eliminates the opportunity for conceptual constructions regarding its intrinsic nature.
That form which was first declared to be empty of the intrinsic nature of form is the negation of the conceptual construction that superimposes an intrinsic nature upon it.
As for that which the Blessed One said— "one perceives neither the arising nor the cessation of phenomena"—
that is a conceptualization of a distinction between those two.
Since names are artificial and the dharmas are designated as such, there is no inherent relationship between word and meaning; therefore, it is held that [the relationship] is not natural.
The attachment of the fool to external objects expands due to delusion;
likewise, this worldly convention exists, yet herein there is no object whatsoever.
In this regard, that object which is conceptualized by him according to its name does not exist in that way;
therefore, the referent of speech is established as being merely a conceptualization of an object according to its name.
The Perfection of Wisdom states that the Buddha, as well as the Bodhisattva, is likewise merely a name; it declares that the conceptualization of the reality of objects is a calamity.
This is a negation of the word and its referent; no real entity is being excluded.
In this same way, the determination of the meaning in other statements should also be understood.
The knower of reality does not correctly perceive any names as being in accordance with their actual referents;
therefore, this does not constitute a refutation of the word.
Subhūti, however, rejected both the word and the meaning of the word;
he said, "I do not perceive even the name of a bodhisattva."
There is no statement in the *Prajñāpāramitā* that is not encompassed by this [method];
however, those meanings must be inferred solely by means of such subtle intelligence.
The rejection of the intended meaning and the conceptualization of another meaning— this, indeed,
is declared in the *Prajñāpāramitā* to be a counterfeit.
This is the summary of the subject matter based upon the Perfection of Wisdom;
that very same subject matter is now repeated again, relying upon further points of meaning.
By whatever merit has been acquired through correctly compiling this *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, may all people attain the perfection of wisdom.
The Compendium of the Essential Meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is completed. This is the work of the venerable master Dignāga.
